title: Measure the retry amplification
hook: How do naive retries turn a blip into an outage, and why is jitter essential?

scenes.caption: Retries can multiply across layers and overload a recovering dependency.
scenes.narration: A dependency slows down, so each layer retries. If three layers each make three attempts, one request can cause twenty seven attempts at the bottom.

elements.text:
# Worst case: all attempts fail
client: 3 attempts
service: 3 attempts per client call
storage: 3 attempts per service call
3 * 3 * 3 = 27

items: Count attempts, not just logical requests

scenes.caption: Transport captures and application metrics answer different questions.
scenes.narration: Capture the lab endpoint while injecting failures. TCP retransmissions are not application retries; use request identifiers and server counters to measure actual request amplification.

elements.text:
sudo tcpdump -ni lo \
  'tcp port 8080' \
  -w retry-lab.pcap
# Match request IDs in app logs

items: Use the interface carrying lab traffic
Encrypted packets do not expose request IDs

scenes.caption: Exponential backoff without jitter can synchronize clients.
scenes.narration: Use a capped exponential window and draw a random delay within it. Bound attempts and the total deadline; backoff alone does not limit accumulated retry load.

items: Add a retry budget or token bucket

scenes.caption: A timeout does not mean the remote operation never committed.
scenes.narration: A timed out payment may already have committed. Reuse an idempotency key and stored result; retry only appropriate failures, then compare recovery time and request counts.

takeaway: Bound retries by attempts and deadline, add jitter, and retry side effects only with idempotency.
